title: Tongue Slip Parlour
pitch: A parlour where sounds trade places. Type any phrase and a rule engine splits every word into onset and rime, tries every swap between word pairs, and ranks the ones where both halves land as real words, drawing the sounds as tiles that physically change seats. Then play the second side: an Untwist puzzle shows a scrambled phrase and the visitor works out the original, with a seeded daily deck and a link that shares the exact puzzle.
whyNow: Timeless: a self-contained language toy with a daily puzzle, no news hook needed. It also fills the owed humor slot with a joke that is a rule the visitor discovers.

research.summary: A spoonerism swaps the opening sounds of two words and is named for William Archibald Spooner (1844 to 1930) of New College, Oxford; several independent results agree, and also agree that nearly all famous quotes credited to him are doubtful (only one is substantiated per the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations as reported), so the page labels its examples traditional or invented. Prior art exists: a Finnish counterpart (sananmuunnos) with a JavaScript solver on GitHub, a phoneme-based Python package and a spelling-based Rust crate (the last two not re-found by the verifier). The verifier found no polished browser puzzle that ranks swaps, but that is a negative from a few searches. Descriptions of the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary licence differ between results (BSD, public domain, unrestricted with acknowledgment), so nothing from it is bundled and the lexicon is hand-written.

facts.claim: The term spoonerism comes from William Archibald Spooner (1844 to 1930), an Oxford don at New College, and names a swap of the initial sounds of two words.

Most spoonerisms credited to Spooner are doubtful or invented; the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations is reported to list only one substantiated example, so the page labels examples traditional or invented.
As of 2026-10-12, per a GitHub listing seen in search: a JavaScript solver for sananmuunnos, the Finnish counterpart of the spoonerism, exists as a port of its author's Python module.
As of 2026-10-12, per Wikipedia as seen in a search summary: Finnish sananmuunnos swaps morae rather than syllables and Finnish suffixes multiply the valid swaps (unconfirmed, single digest).

Search results describe the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary licence differently (BSD per Wikipedia, public domain per a GitHub repackaging, unrestricted use with acknowledgment per the original licence file), so the project bundles none of it.

design.coreLoop: Type or pick a phrase, watch the engine split it into onset and rime tiles and propose ranked swaps. Pick one and the tiles trade seats with a short animation and a read-aloud button. In Untwist mode a scrambled phrase appears and the visitor drags sound tiles back to restore the original; hints reveal which word pair was swapped. Mastery comes from learning the engine's rules (digraphs, silent letters, how vowels start a word) and a codex fills with rare finds. Daily deck and shareable hash keep it fresh.
sophisticationHooks: Rule engine: orthographic onset/rime splitter with a digraph and exception table (ph, kn, wr, qu, sh, ch, th, silent h, vowel starts), then a swap search over all word pairs and positions in the phrase
Swap scoring: both outputs real words in the bundled lexicon, tile weight, part-of-speech plausibility and a clean-humour filter; ranked results with a visible 'why this scored' breakdown
Untwist puzzle: seeded daily deck of invented phrases, three difficulty tiers, hint ladder, streak kept in localStorage with try/catch, sharable result and puzzle via URL hash
Sound-tile animation in SVG with reduced-motion fallback, optional read-aloud through the browser's built-in speech voices
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: a curated lexicon of about 1,200 common words chosen to be swap-fertile (onset/rime derived by the splitter from spelling, with an exception table for digraphs and silent letters, plus part-of-speech tags), the splitter and swap engine as a pure module with a node test file, parlour view with tile animation, Untwist puzzle with about 80 hand-written phrases that a script confirms the engine can solve uniquely, codex, about panel. Unknown words are flagged and the empty state offers curated starter phrases. Cut: multi-language modes, user word lists, sound effects, any server, anything beyond a basic read-aloud button.
risks: With a small bundled lexicon, a typed phrase will often yield few or no valid swaps: the empty state must be charming, suggest starters and say which words are unknown, and the lexicon is chosen for swap-fertility rather than size.
Spelling-based onset detection misjudges some words; an exception table and a rule that only swaps whose results are in the lexicon are offered limit this.
Famous Spooner quotes are doubtful (confirmed by several results): all examples are labelled traditional or invented and nothing is quoted as documented.
Humour must stay mild: lexicon and phrase bank are original and checked for slurs and crude pairs by a script.
Speech voices vary by device: read-aloud is optional and uses only the browser's built-in voices.

Distinctness from existing toys is only lightly checked: prior art (Finnish solver, Python package, Rust crate) exists and no polished ranked-swap puzzle was found in a few searches, which is not proof; the Finnish and phoneme-tool details are shown as reported, per source, as of 2026-10-12, or omitted.

verification.notes: Namesake, dates and doubtful-quote caution agree across Wikipedia, Straight Dope, alt-usage and Quote Investigator results; no page opened (DNS failures). Lexicon shrunk to about 1,200 words and 80 phrases; the main risk is that typed phrases rarely yield swaps.
